name: Harken Energy

summary.text: Harken Energy Corporation (earlier Harken Oil and Gas) was a Dallas-area oil and gas company. In September 1986 it acquired Spectrum 7, a troubled company run by George W. Bush, in a stock swap, and Bush joined Harken's board, where he served from 1986 until October 1993. Its investors in the late 1980s included Harvard Management Company's venture arm Aeneas Venture Corp. and Saudi investor Abdullah Taha Bakhsh, whose representative Talat Othman sat on the board. In January 1990 a Harken subsidiary signed a production sharing agreement with the Bahrain National Oil Company for offshore exploration; Bass Enterprises funded the drilling, and both wells were dry. Bush's June 22, 1990 sale of 212,140 Harken shares, disclosed late, was investigated by the SEC from April 1991; the SEC closed the inquiry in October 1993 without enforcement action, stating that the termination was not to be construed as an exoneration.

facts.claim: On September 22, 1986, Harken announced it had bought Spectrum 7, the oil company George W. Bush ran, and Bush joined Harken's board of directors. Spectrum 7 had posted losses of $400,000 six months earlier and carried about $3 million of debt; the Spectrum 7 sellers received about $2 million in Harken stock, of which Bush's share was reported at about $500,000, plus a consulting contract and stock options.
facts.quote: On September 22, 1986, Harken announced it had bought Spectrum 7, and Bush joined the board of directors.

sources.title: A brief history of Bush, Harken and the SEC
Right on the money: The George W. Bush profile

facts.claim: The Washington Post reported in 1999 that Harken acquired Bush with Spectrum 7 and used him not as an operating manager but as a high-profile board member; a former Spectrum 7 president said the company believed having his name there would be a big help. Bush received more than $300,000 of Harken stock, options to buy more, and a consulting contract.
facts.quote: Harken also acquired Bush, whom it used not as an operating manager but as a high-profile board member.

sources.title: Bush Name Helps Fuel Oil Dealings

facts.claim: About a month after Bush joined the board, Harvard Management Company, which manages Harvard University's endowment, invested in Harken through its venture arm Aeneas Venture Corp., which agreed to invest $20 million in Harken and buy $2 million of newly issued Harken stock. Harvard's stake later rose to about 30 percent, and Michael Eisenson represented Harvard on Harken's board.
facts.quote: Barely a month after Bush came aboard, the company received a huge capital infusion from Harvard Management Company, which manages Harvard University's vast endowment.

sources.title: A brief history of Bush, Harken and the SEC
Harken's Ivy League underwriter

facts.claim: On December 3, 1990, Harvard's Aeneas Venture Corp. announced a joint venture with Harken, the Harken Anadarko Partnership, in which Harvard took an 84 percent stake and Harken 16 percent. The Boston Globe later reported that Harvard invested roughly $50 million in Harken in all and that the position contributed to the endowment's largest-ever loss in 1991; the Globe found no evidence that the investment was a political favor to the Bush family.
facts.quote: Harvard's venture arm, Aeneas Venture Corp., announced it was entering into a joint venture with Harken on December 3 of 1990. Under the agreement, known as the Harken Anadarko Partnership, Harvard took an 84 percent stake and Harken 16 percent.

sources.title: Harken's Ivy League underwriter
Globe: Harvard invested $50 million in Harken

facts.claim: Mother Jones reported in 1992 that Harken's $25 million stock offering in 1987 was underwritten by Stephens, Inc., a Little Rock brokerage, which placed the stock with the London subsidiary of Union Bank. The same reporting said Saudi investor Sheikh Abdullah Bakhsh bought a block of Harken stock and placed his representative, Talat Othman, on Harken's board.
facts.quote: Harken's $25 million stock offering in 1987 was underwritten by Stephens, Inc., a Little Rock brokerage, which placed the stock with the London subsidiary of Union Bank.

facts.claim: Salon reported that two years after the 1986 merger, Abdullah Taha Bakhsh, a former director of Saudi Arabia's income tax department, purchased an 11 percent stake in Harken through his company Traco International. Time reported that Bakhsh bought an 11 percent stake the year after Bush joined the board; Mother Jones put his holding at 17.6 percent. SEC filings list Talat M. Othman as a Harken director.
facts.quote: Two years after the merger, Abdullah Taha Bakhsh, a former director of Saudi Arabia's income tax department, purchased an 11 percent stake in Harken through his company Traco International.

facts.claim: In January 1990, Harken's wholly owned subsidiary Harken Bahrain Oil Company entered into a production sharing agreement with the Bahrain National Oil Company giving it exclusive exploration rights over most of Bahrain's offshore territory, with a 35-year term subject to discovery. In July 1990, Bass Enterprises Production Company joined a joint venture and committed to fund at least the first three exploratory wells.
facts.quote: In January 1990, Harken, through its wholly-owned subsidiary, Harken Bahrain Oil Company ("HBOC"), entered into a production sharing agreement with the Bahrain National Oil Company ("BANOCO").

sources.title: Harken Energy Corp, Form 10-K for fiscal year 1993
Harken Energy Corp, Form 10-K for fiscal year 1994

facts.claim: The Bahrain wells were dry. Drilling of the Jarim No. 2 well began in November 1991 and in March 1992 Harken announced it was not productive of oil or gas; in February 1993 the Muharraq No. 1 well was plugged and abandoned. On April 8, 1993, Bass Enterprises was released from further drilling obligations and paid Harken Bahrain Oil Company about $2 million; Harken let portions of the acreage expire in February and August 1993.
facts.quote: On April 8, 1993, HBOC and BEPCO entered into an agreement whereby BEPCO was released and discharged from any future drilling obligations related to HBOC's production sharing agreement, and the joint venture agreement between HBOC and BEPCO was terminated.

sources.title: Harken Energy Corp, Form 10-K for fiscal year 1993

facts.claim: The Washington Post reported in 1999 that Bahrain's then minister of development and industry, Yousuf Shirawi, said he went looking for a small American company and found Harken through Houston oil consultant Michael Ameen, a longtime friend, and that he was unaware of Bush's board seat at the time. Harken had never drilled overseas or offshore, and the Post reported that Bush warned fellow directors against the project at board meetings.
facts.quote: Shirawi said he decided to go shopping for a small American company and found Harken through a Houston oil consultant and longtime friend, Michael Ameen.

sources.title: Bush: The Making of a Candidate (Harken sidebar)
A Baseless Suspicion

facts.claim: The Center for Public Integrity noted that Harken signed the Bahrain agreement despite never having drilled an oil well overseas, that rumors tied the award to Bush's father, and that no proof of this has been offered. The Wall Street Journal asked in 1991 whether the contract reflected an effort to cozy up to a presidential son; Harken's Monte Swetnam said the Bahrainis knew Bush sat on the board and was the President's son.
facts.quote: Despite never having drilled an oil well overseas, Harken penned an agreement with the Bahraini government to explore and develop petroleum offshore. Rumors tied the choice to Bush's father, but no proof has ever been offered.

facts.claim: Harken lent Bush $180,375 in 1986 and 1988 to buy Harken stock, according to SEC filings cited by the Washington Post: $96,000 in 1986 for 80,000 shares and $84,375 in 1988 for 25,000 shares. The loans carried 5 percent interest, reported as two and a half points below the prevailing market rate; in 1989 the company lifted Bush's personal liability on them, and he later retired the debt by surrendering 105,000 shares held as collateral.
facts.quote: Bush accepted loans totaling $180,375 from Harken Energy Corp. in 1986 and 1988, according to Securities and Exchange Commission filings.

sources.title: Bush Took Oil Firm's Loans as Director

Bush Took Sweetheart Loans

facts.claim: On June 22, 1990, Bush sold his 212,140 Harken shares at $4 a share, about eight days before the end of a second quarter in which Harken lost about $23 million; the loss was announced on August 20, 1990. Sources give the proceeds as $848,560 (the figure in Bush's Form 4, per the SEC memo) or about $835,307 net (the figure in his notice of proposed sale, per the Washington Post).
facts.quote: The largest sale was his Form 4 report disclosing that he had sold $848,560 of Harken stock on June 22, 1990, just weeks before the company filed a quarterly report revealing that it had hemorrhaged $23 million during that period.

sources.title: A brief history of Bush, Harken and the SEC
Bush Name Helps Fuel Oil Dealings

facts.claim: A week before Bush's June 1990 sale, Harken's outside lawyers cautioned Bush and other directors against selling shares if they had significant negative information about the company's prospects, the Washington Post reported in 2002. Bush had said he obtained clearance from Harken's general counsel to sell. Salon reported in 2002 that internal Harken memos showed the company had lost $28.5 million in trade credit since January 1, 1990, with another $11.8 million in jeopardy.
facts.quote: A week before George W. Bush's 1990 sale of stock in Harken Energy Co., the firm's outside lawyers cautioned Bush and other directors against selling shares if they had significant negative information about the company's prospects.

sources.title: Bush Sold Stock After Lawyers' Warning
Memos: Bush knew of Harken's problems

facts.claim: The SEC's Division of Enforcement opened an investigation of Bush's Harken sale on April 5, 1991, the day after the Wall Street Journal reported he had filed the required insider-transaction form about eight months late. The SEC memo noted that Bush had filed late Form 4s on four occasions involving Harken stock worth more than $1 million. The Washington Post reported the June 1990 sale was disclosed 34 weeks late.
facts.quote: Bush, the SEC memo noted, had on four occasions filed late Form 4s involving Harken stock worth more than $1 million.

sources.title: A brief history of Bush, Harken and the SEC

facts.claim: An August 21, 1991 SEC staff memo stated that there was insufficient evidence to establish three necessary aspects of a possible insider trading case, and a March 18, 1992 enforcement action memorandum summarized the investigation's findings. According to the Center for Public Integrity's summary of the SEC records, investigators concluded that neither Bush nor the rest of Harken's leadership were aware of the magnitude of the loss at the time he sold; the SEC never interviewed Bush.
facts.quote: The staff's investigation indicates that there is insufficient evidence to establish three necessary aspects of a possible insider trading case.

facts.claim: On October 18, 1993, the SEC notified Bush's lawyer that the investigation had been terminated as to the conduct of Mr. Bush and that no enforcement action was contemplated with respect to him. The letter added that the termination must in no way be construed as indicating that the party has been exonerated or that no action may ultimately result from the investigation.
facts.quote: must in no way be construed as indicating that the party has been exonerated or that no action may ultimately result

facts.claim: The SEC separately directed Harken to correct its financial reports over its 1989 sale of the Aloha Petroleum subsidiary, which had been financed by a seller loan and used to book a gain; the Center for Public Integrity reported that the company had effectively concealed losses by selling a retail subsidiary through a seller-financed loan, and that the SEC forced the company to amend its books to reflect the hidden losses.
facts.quote: The company effectively concealed the hemorrhaging by selling a retail subsidiary through a seller-financed loan.

facts.claim: Bush resigned from Harken's board effective October 26, 1993 and terminated the consulting agreement under which he had served as a consultant to Harken since April 1987, according to Harken's 1994 proxy statement.
facts.quote: Bush resigned from Harken's Board of Directors effective October 26, 1993 and terminated the Consulting Agreement under which he had served as a consultant to Harken since April 1987.

openQuestions: The owner's claim that money went to Bush from a UAE account is not supported by any source found in this session. The financing documented for Harken came from Harvard Management Company (US), Abdullah Taha Bakhsh (Saudi Arabia, via Traco International), a 1987 offering placed through Stephens, Inc. with a London subsidiary of Union Bank (Swiss), Bass Enterprises (US) for the Bahrain drilling, and the Bahrain government contract. Bush's own money came from Harken's loans to him and his 1990 stock sale; no source names a UAE account, Abu Dhabi, or a transfer from BCCI or its shareholders to Bush or to Harken.

The task asked for the Senate BCCI report's description of Union Bank of Switzerland's stake in Harken via a BCCI-linked arrangement. Three searches of irp.fas.org returned no Harken passage; the report's chapters found describe BCCI's secretly controlled Geneva affiliate Banque de Commerce et de Placements but not a UBS-Harken link. The owner should check the full report (S. Prt. 102-140) before asserting that the Senate report ties Harken's financing to BCCI. The crash-conduits node's phrase 'capital from BCCI-connected financiers' therefore rests on secondary reporting (Mother Jones 1992 on Bakhsh's banker), not on the Senate record found here.

The site's node lists Ghaith Pharaon and SEC Chairman Richard Breeden as Harken 'insiders'. No source found links Pharaon to Harken. Breeden's role in the Bush inquiry was not researched; the SEC documents found are staff memos (August 1991, March 1992) and an October 1993 letter from the Division of Enforcement.
The site's node says Harken's stock fell 25 percent after the loss disclosure; this figure was not verified in this session.

Mother Jones (1992) says 'Union Bank', not 'Union Bank of Switzerland'; the Swiss identification comes from less reliable secondary accounts. The connection is recorded as 'reported' on that basis and should be confirmed against the original Wall Street Journal (1991) reporting.

The Washington Post Bahrain reporting (Shirawi, Ameen, Bush's objections) is attributed here to the Post's July 30, 1999 Harken sidebar (bushside073099.htm) as returned by search; the owner should confirm that the quoted passages appear in that article rather than in the companion piece.
The Harken Bahrain agreement is dated January 1990 in Harken's SEC filings; Salon's 2001 article places the contract in 1988, the year of Bakhsh's investment. The SEC filing date is used here.
The Senate BCCI report has not been found to describe the 1987 Harken offering; the Union Bank of Switzerland identification rests on secondary accounts.
